unit.title: The Jesus Lens
unit.summary: How the Old and New Testaments fit together, how Jesus and Paul read the Scriptures, and what it means that Jesus is the Word who interprets the words. This unit gives full voice to the “Jesus is perfect theology” reading (Christ as the full revelation of the Father) and sets it beside other Christ-centred readings — Reformed, evangelical, Catholic and Orthodox — with Jewish perspectives and the fair critiques of each.

lessons.title: Old and New: Progressive Revelation (and Progressive Christianity)
lessons.question: How do the Old and New Testaments fit together? Is “progressive revelation” the same thing as liberal or “progressive” Christianity?
lessons.bigIdea: The two Testaments tell one story: God spoke truly “in many portions and in many ways”, and then finally and fully in his Son. Progressive revelation means God’s self-disclosure unfolds and reaches its peak in Jesus; progressive Christianity usually means the church’s moral knowledge moves on beyond the text. They are different claims, and most views sit somewhere on a spectrum between them.

sections.heading: One story in two parts
sections.body:
Christians call the two halves of the Bible the Old Testament and the New Testament. “Testament” translates a Latin word for “covenant”. The names come from the Bible itself: Jeremiah promised a “new covenant” written on the heart, and Jesus spoke of the cup at the Last Supper as “the new covenant in my blood”.

The New Testament never treats the Old as a separate religion. It opens with a genealogy that runs from Abraham to Jesus, and it quotes or echoes the Hebrew Scriptures hundreds of times. When Paul says “all Scripture is God-breathed” and “able to make you wise unto salvation”, the Scriptures he means are what we call the Old Testament. Jewish readers rightly point out that “Old” can sound like “out of date”; some Christians therefore say “Hebrew Bible” or “First Testament”. The word “old” here means “first” and “earlier”, not “worthless”.

So the first thing to hold is continuity: one God, one people-story, one promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s family, carried forward to its fulfilment.

sections.heading: What is genuinely new
sections.body:
The second thing to hold is newness. Something happens in Jesus that the earlier Scriptures did not contain on their own. John puts it simply: “the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.” Hebrews says the first covenant is “becoming obsolete” and that the law had “a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things”.

In practice the New Testament reports real changes: animal sacrifice ends because of Christ’s once-for-all offering; food laws no longer divide Jew and Gentile; circumcision is not required of Gentile believers; the people of God is now defined by trust in the Messiah and the gift of the Spirit rather than by ethnic descent. Even Jesus’ first followers found these changes hard (see Peter’s vision in Acts 10 and the Jerusalem council in Acts 15).

The question every Christian tradition has to answer is how continuity and newness fit together. Too much continuity and Christ becomes a footnote to Moses. Too much newness and the Old Testament becomes a different religion with a different God — the error the early church called Marcionism.

sections.heading: “In many portions and in many ways”: progressive revelation
sections.body:
Hebrews opens with a sentence that frames this whole unit: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.” The two Greek words behind “sundry times and divers manners” (*polymerōs* and *polytropōs*) mean “in many parts” and “in many ways”. The earlier word was real, inspired speech from God, but it came in pieces, through many people, in many forms — law, story, poem, vision.

“Progressive revelation” is the theological name for this pattern. It means God made himself known step by step across history, and that later stages clarify and complete earlier ones. Peter says the prophets “searched diligently” about a salvation they did not fully see. Paul speaks of a “mystery” hidden for ages and now revealed. Jesus is the last and fullest word: not one more prophet, but the Son through whom God speaks.

This idea is not new or liberal. Irenaeus in the second century spoke of God training humanity gradually, like a teacher with children. Reformed theologians such as Geerhardus Vos made “progressive revelation” a key idea of biblical theology, and Catholic teaching (*Dei Verbum* 15) speaks of the Old Testament as showing a “divine pedagogy” — God teaching step by step.

sections.heading: Progressive revelation is not the same as progressive Christianity
sections.body:
The learner’s notes rightly separate two things that are often confused because they share a word.

Progressive revelation says: God’s self-revelation unfolds within Scripture and culminates in Christ. The measure is inside the story — Jesus himself, as the apostles witness to him.

Progressive (or liberal) Christianity is a broad modern movement. Many in it say that the church’s moral and spiritual understanding keeps growing beyond the biblical text, so that some biblical teachings can be set aside in the light of modern knowledge, experience and reason. Thinkers such as Marcus Borg and John Shelby Spong are often named here; they would describe this as honest faith, not unbelief.

The key question that separates them is: what is the final measure? For progressive revelation, it is God’s self-disclosure in Jesus Christ, attested by the apostles. For many progressive Christians, it is the community’s developing conscience, which may read Jesus too as one stage on the road. In real life, views sit on a spectrum (see the visual), and people argue about where particular teachers belong. A fair reader names the measure each one actually uses, rather than labelling them.

sections.heading: Where the “Jesus lens” fits
sections.body:
The learner holds a strong Christ-centred view: Jesus is the full and final revelation of God, so the whole Bible must be read through him (“Jesus is perfect theology”). On this view, the Old Testament is a true, inspired and honest record of God working with people whose perception of him was still partial — “seeing through a glass, darkly”. Jesus is the moment God shows who he has been all along.

Defenders of this view (for example Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak and Brian Zahnd) insist that it is a form of progressive revelation, not progressive Christianity: the measure is not modern taste but the crucified and risen Christ. They also note that John 16 promises the Spirit will lead into “all truth” by taking what belongs to Jesus — not by moving beyond him.

Critics answer that, in practice, deciding what is “Christlike” can quietly import modern values, and that the line between the two can blur. Those debates come in lessons 17–19. For now, the point to hold is that the question “Is it Christlike?” and the question “Is it modern?” are different questions.

visuals.title: From progressive revelation to progressive Christianity
visuals.intro: How do later stages relate to earlier ones, and what is the final measure? Positions are rough; many people mix them.
visuals.left: Revelation unfolds and culminates in Christ; every earlier stage is true revelation
visuals.right: The church’s moral knowledge moves beyond the biblical text

stops.label: Classic progressive revelation
stops.who: Geerhardus Vos, Walter Kaiser, Graeme Goldsworthy, Edmund Clowney
stops.text: God reveals himself in stages; later stages complete earlier ones but never correct them. Every Old Testament statement about God is true for its stage, and Christ is the goal toward which it all moves.

stops.label: Divine pedagogy and accommodation
stops.who: Irenaeus, John Calvin, *Dei Verbum* 15, Paul Copan
stops.text: God stoops to people’s level, like a teacher with children. Some laws were concessions to “hardness of heart” (Matt 19:8) and were temporary. But the record of what God said and did is true; the change is in the people, not in God’s word.

stops.label: Reading backwards (Christotelic / figural)
stops.who: Richard Hays, early Peter Enns, N. T. Wright
stops.text: The Old Testament makes its full sense only when read backwards from the cross and resurrection. Christ is the goal (Greek *telos*) of the story, and the story keeps its own integrity as Israel’s story.

stops.label: Redemptive-movement (trajectory) reading
stops.text: Many biblical laws improved on their surrounding cultures; the direction of travel points toward an “ultimate ethic” beyond the letter of some texts (e.g. slavery). The measure is the text’s own trajectory, completed in Christ.

stops.label: Cruciform Jesus lens
stops.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Tommy Miller; the slogan “Jesus is perfect theology” (Bill Johnson)
stops.text: Jesus, and especially the cross, is the full revelation of God. Portraits of God in the Old Testament that do not look like Jesus reflect the partial, culturally conditioned perception of the people through whom God worked. The Bible is still inspired; Christ is its interpreter.

stops.label: Textual God and actual God
stops.text: Distinguishes the God portrayed in some texts from the God who actually is, and uses Jesus’ teaching as the main test. Openly says some biblical portrayals are mistaken.

stops.label: Progressive Christianity
stops.who: Marcus Borg, John Shelby Spong (in different ways)
stops.text: Scripture is a human response to the sacred. Moral understanding grows through history, experience and science; many biblical teachings, and some traditional doctrines about Jesus, can be revised.

visuals.title: Continuity and newness between the Testaments
visuals.intro: What carries over, and what changes in Christ?

rows.label: Covenant

rows.label: Sacrifice and temple

“He declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19); Peter’s vision (Acts 10)

Poured out on “all flesh” (Acts 2:17, quoting Joel)

visuals.title: “Many portions, many ways”: revelation in stages
visuals.intro: A simplified view of how Scripture presents God’s self-disclosure unfolding. Dates are approximate and some are debated.

events.label: Promise to Abraham
events.text: Blessing for all nations through one family (Gen 12:1-3). Date approximate and debated.

events.label: Exodus and Sinai
events.text: God reveals his name and gives the law within a covenant of rescue (Exod 3; Exod 20). The date of the exodus is debated (c. 1446 or c. 1260 BC).

events.label: David and the psalms
events.text: Promise of a lasting king (2 Sam 7:12-16); Israel learns to pray and lament.

events.label: The prophets
events.text: Mercy over sacrifice (Hos 6:6), justice (Amos 5:24), a servant who suffers (Isa 53).

events.label: Exile and a new covenant promised
events.text: Jerusalem falls; Jeremiah and Ezekiel promise a new heart and a new covenant (Jer 31:31-34; Ezek 36:26-27).

events.label: The Son
events.text: God speaks “by his Son”, the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:1-3). Crucifixion and resurrection (c. AD 30 or 33).

events.label: The apostles interpret
events.text: Paul and the other apostles read the Scriptures in the light of Christ and the Spirit (Acts 15; 2 Cor 3).

voices.text: The New is in the Old concealed; the Old is in the New revealed.
God, the inspirer and author of both Testaments, wisely arranged that the New Testament be hidden in the Old and the Old be made manifest in the New.

views.name: Classic progressive revelation (salvation-history)
views.who: Geerhardus Vos, Walter Kaiser, Graeme Goldsworthy, Edmund Clowney, D. A. Carson
views.summary: God revealed himself in historical stages. Each stage is true and authoritative for its moment; later stages fulfil and explain earlier ones. Christ is the climax, and the Old Testament remains God’s word to the church, read in the light of its fulfilment.
views.strengths: Takes both Testaments as fully God’s word; follows the pattern of Heb 1:1-3 and Luke 24:27; guards strongly against Marcionism.
views.critiques: Can struggle to explain Old Testament portraits of God that seem unlike Jesus, and may treat hard texts as simply “true for then” without wrestling with them.

views.name: Divine pedagogy and accommodation
views.who: Irenaeus, Origen, John Chrysostom, John Calvin, Catholic teaching in *Dei Verbum* 15
views.summary: God accommodated himself to the capacity of his hearers, teaching humanity as a patient teacher teaches children. Some Old Testament provisions were “incomplete and temporary” concessions, yet they were a real part of God’s teaching plan.
views.strengths: Rooted in Jesus’ own words about Moses and “hardness of heart” (Matt 19:8); has deep roots in the church fathers and in Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed theology.
views.critiques: Leaves open how far accommodation goes: did God only permit some customs, or did he also allow himself to be portrayed in ways that were not true of him? Traditions disagree.

views.name: Jesus lens (Christocentric, cruciform)
views.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Tommy Miller; “Jesus is perfect theology” (Bill Johnson)
views.summary: Jesus is not one stage among others but the full and final revelation of the Father. The Old Testament is an inspired, honest record of a people’s developing and partly flawed perception of the one God who has always been like Jesus.
views.strengths: Takes John 1:18, John 14:9 and Heb 1:3 with full seriousness; offers a way through texts of violence; keeps the measure inside the canon (Christ), not modern opinion.
views.critiques: Critics say it can drift toward Marcion by setting parts of the Old Testament against Jesus; that the New Testament also contains judgement texts; and that “Christlike” can become whatever the reader prefers.

views.name: Progressive (liberal) Christianity
views.who: Marcus Borg, John Shelby Spong, many mainline Protestant writers
views.summary: The Bible is a human, historical witness to experiences of God. Moral and spiritual insight continues to grow, and the church may revise biblical teaching in the light of reason, science and experience.
views.strengths: Honest about the human side of Scripture and about texts that have been used to harm; seeks a faith that is intellectually credible today.
views.critiques: Traditional Christians (and Jesus-lens teachers) argue that it replaces Christ with the modern conscience as the final measure, and can lose the uniqueness of Jesus that the New Testament proclaims.

views.name: Jewish readings of the Hebrew Bible
views.who: Jon Levenson, Amy-Jill Levine, Marc Zvi Brettler
views.summary: The Hebrew Bible is complete Scripture in its own right, read through the Jewish interpretive tradition (Mishnah, Talmud, midrash). It is not an “Old” Testament waiting for something else.
views.strengths: Reminds Christians that these texts were Israel’s Scripture first and have their own voice; warns against calling Judaism “old” or superseded.
views.critiques: Christians believe Jesus and the apostles read the same texts as pointing to the Messiah (Luke 24:27); the two communities read the same words through different keys.

misreadings.topic: “The Old Testament God and the New Testament God”
misreadings.popular: The Old Testament shows an angry God of law and the New Testament shows a loving God of grace.
misreadings.inContext: Both Testaments speak of the same God who is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger” (Exod 34:6). Grace runs through the Old Testament (the exodus comes before the law), and judgement appears in the New. The real question is not two Gods but how God’s one character is revealed in stages and finally in Jesus. Jesus-lens writers such as Jersak and Boyd reject the “two Gods” idea just as firmly as traditional scholars do.
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars (e.g. Christopher J. H. Wright, Paul Copan) stress that the Old Testament is full of mercy and that the New Testament still speaks of wrath (John 3:36; Rom 1:18). They warn that the popular contrast repeats Marcion’s error.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If we picture two Gods, we will either ignore half the Bible or fear the Father while loving the Son. Both Testaments ask us to know one God.

misreadings.topic: “Progressive revelation means the Bible is out of date”
misreadings.popular: If revelation is progressive, then later understanding (including ours) can correct the Bible.
misreadings.inContext: In Hebrews, the progression ends in the Son: God has spoken “in these last days” by him. The movement is toward Christ, not beyond him. Progressive revelation is a classic, conservative idea found in the church fathers and in Reformed theology.
misreadings.defence: Many evangelical scholars add that later stages never contradict earlier ones; they complete them. Jesus-lens writers would agree that Christ is the end point, but they allow that people’s perception of God in some earlier texts was partial.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Confusing the two words leads some to reject a healthy Christ-centred reading as “liberal”, and leads others to treat their own culture as the final word.

discuss: Before this lesson, did you think of the Old Testament as describing a different kind of God? Where did that picture come from?
Name one thing that clearly carries over from the Old Testament to the New, and one thing that clearly changes. How does the New Testament itself explain the change?
What is the difference between saying “God revealed himself step by step” and saying “we now know better than the Bible”?
On the spectrum visual, where would you place yourself today? What is the final measure you actually use when two texts seem to clash?
How might Jewish friends feel about the word “Old”? How can Christians speak about the Hebrew Bible respectfully?
practice: Read Hebrews 1:1-4 slowly three times. Write down every word that describes what God did in the past and every word that describes the Son.
Pick one Old Testament law (e.g. Lev 11 or Deut 24:1-4) and trace what the New Testament does with it. Note whether the change is described as fulfilment, concession, or something else.
Read Exodus 34:6-7 and then John 1:14-18. List the words the two passages share (glory, grace, truth) and talk about what John is claiming.

lessons.title: How Jesus and Paul Read the Scriptures
lessons.question: How did Jesus and Paul bring clarity to the Old Testament Scriptures — and what does their way of reading teach us about how to read?
lessons.bigIdea: Jesus did not read the Scriptures as a flat rule book. He read them as a story about himself, put mercy at the centre, named concessions as concessions, and sometimes said “but I say to you”. Paul, after meeting the risen Christ, said the same Scriptures stay veiled until we turn to the Lord.

sections.heading: Jesus read the Scriptures as being about him
sections.body:
After the resurrection, Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples to Emmaus. “Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.” Later that evening he told the gathered disciples that everything written “in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms” about him had to be fulfilled — the three parts of the Hebrew Bible.

To religious leaders who knew the Scriptures well, he said: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” The problem was not too much Bible study. It was Bible study that never arrived at the person the Bible points to.

This is the starting point for everything else in this lesson: for Jesus, the Scriptures are a witness, and he is the one they witness to.

sections.heading: “You have heard that it was said… but I say to you”
sections.body:
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says six times, “Ye have heard that it was said… but I say unto you.” Some of what “was said” is a direct quotation of the law (“thou shalt not kill”; “an eye for an eye”); some is a popular addition (“hate thine enemy” is not in the law). In each case Jesus goes deeper than the letter: from murder to anger, from adultery to lust, from limited revenge to no revenge, from loving neighbours to loving enemies.

Scholars read this in two main ways. Many evangelical and Jewish scholars say Jesus is not overturning Moses but recovering the law’s true intent against narrow interpretations — after all, he has just said he came “not to destroy, but to fulfil” and that not one stroke of the law will pass away. Others (including Jesus-lens writers) point out that in at least one case — “an eye for an eye” was God’s own legal command, not a misreading — Jesus moves beyond what the text required, speaking with an authority that belongs to God alone. The crowds noticed: he taught “as one having authority, and not as the scribes.”

Both readings agree on the heart of it: Jesus himself is the authoritative interpreter of the law, and the direction he takes it is toward the Father’s mercy — “that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.”

sections.heading: Mercy as the key: Nazareth, Samaria and the dinner table
sections.body:
In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus read from Isaiah 61. He stopped in the middle of a sentence: after “to preach the acceptable year of the Lord”, he closed the scroll before the next words, “and the day of vengeance of our God”. Then he said, “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.” Readers have long asked why he stopped there (see the lenses visual).

When a Samaritan village refused to welcome him, James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven — as Elijah had done to soldiers sent by King Ahaziah. Jesus “turned, and rebuked them.” Some later manuscripts add, “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of”; the earliest manuscripts do not have these words, so most modern translations put them in a footnote. Either way, Jesus refused a method that one Old Testament story had used.

When he was criticised for eating with tax collectors and sinners, he quoted Hosea: “Go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.” He quoted the same verse again when his disciples were accused of breaking the sabbath. “Go and learn” was a phrase teachers used for sending students back to a text; Jesus was telling experts in the Scriptures that they had missed the point of them.

sections.heading: Concessions, foods and the sabbath: what the law was for
sections.body:
When asked about divorce, Jesus answered that “Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” Here Jesus himself says that a provision in the law of Moses was a concession to human hardness, not a picture of God’s ideal. He then reads Genesis 1–2 as the deeper word.

In Mark 7, Jesus teaches that what goes into a person does not make them unclean, but what comes out of the heart. Mark adds a comment: “Thus he declared all foods clean” (the wording of most modern translations; the KJV reads “purging all meats”). Acts shows the church taking time to grasp this. Jesus also said, “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath” — the law serves human life, not the other way round.

Taken together, these show a pattern: Jesus asks what a command was for, and what it reveals about the Father’s heart. He keeps the law’s purpose and sets aside readings that work against it.

sections.heading: Irony and sharp words against religious readings
sections.body:
The learner’s notes observe that Jesus used sarcasm and contradicted religious views. The Gospels show this clearly, though “irony” is often the more accurate word. “Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mark 7:9) is biting irony. “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” is a comic picture of careful rule-keeping that misses “judgment, mercy, and faith”. “It cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem” is sharp irony about a city that kills its prophets.

Two cautions keep this fair. First, these were arguments inside Judaism, between Jews, in the style of the prophets — not attacks on Jewish people or on the Torah. Many Pharisees shared Jesus’ concern for mercy, and some later followed him. Second, Jesus’ target is a way of reading that uses Scripture to protect status and exclude others. Christians are just as capable of that today.

sections.heading: Paul: the veil, the guardian and the goal
sections.body:
Paul was a highly trained reader of Scripture before he met Christ. Afterwards he did not throw the Scriptures away; he reread them. In 2 Corinthians 3 he says that when the old covenant is read, “the same vail” that covered Moses’ face lies over the reader’s heart, and “when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away.” He contrasts “the letter” that “killeth” with “the spirit” that “giveth life”. This is not a contrast between literal and spiritual meanings, but between a covenant written on stone and the new covenant written by the Spirit on hearts.

In Galatians 3, Paul calls the law a *paidagōgos* — a household slave who guarded and escorted a child until he came of age (KJV “schoolmaster”). It had a real, good, temporary role “unto Christ”. In Galatians 4 he reads the story of Sarah and Hagar figuratively. In Romans 10:4 he says “Christ is the end of the law”; the Greek *telos* can mean “end”, “goal” or both, and scholars debate which Paul means. In 1 Corinthians 10 he says Israel’s wilderness stories “happened unto them for ensamples (*typoi*, patterns): and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.”

Paul still calls the law “holy, and just, and good”. His point is that the Scriptures find their goal and their meaning in Christ.

visuals.intro: Eight places where Jesus engaged an Old Testament text or a common reading of it.

visuals.title: Why did Jesus stop reading?
visuals.intro: Luke 4:18-19 quotes Isa 61:1-2 but ends before “the day of vengeance of our God”. Four ways of reading the gap.
visuals.passage: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor… to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. [Isaiah continues: “and the day of vengeance of our God”.]

lenses.name: Jesus lens
lenses.who: Brian Zahnd, Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak
lenses.reading: The pause is deliberate and revealing. Jesus announces God’s favour and leaves vengeance out. The crowd turns hostile when he says God’s favour reaches Gentiles (the widow of Zarephath, Naaman). He is showing what the Father is truly like.

lenses.name: Two comings
lenses.reading: Jesus stops because his first coming fulfils the year of favour; the day of judgement belongs to his return (2 Thess 1:7-9). The omission is about timing, not a rejection of vengeance.

lenses.name: Jubilee and Jewish background
lenses.who: Scholars of Second Temple Judaism; Jewish readers
lenses.reading: Isa 61 draws on the Jubilee year of release (Lev 25). In Isaiah, the “day of vengeance” is God’s rescue of his oppressed people from their oppressors. Luke also blends in a line from Isa 58:6 (“to set at liberty them that are bruised”), so this is a shaped summary, not a word-for-word reading.

lenses.name: Luke as author
lenses.reading: Luke has crafted this scene as the programme for his whole Gospel: good news to the poor, release, and inclusion of outsiders. The selection of lines reflects Luke’s themes, whatever exactly was read that day.

visuals.title: Who said it — and what kind of reading is it?
visuals.intro: Sort each saying by the move it makes with Scripture.

categories.label: Reads Scripture as pointing to Christ
Recovers the purpose behind a command
Moves beyond the letter of a command

items.text: “They are they which testify of me.”
items.why: Jesus names himself as the subject the Scriptures witness to.

items.text: “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.”
items.why: Jesus asks what the sabbath is for and reads the commands in that light.

items.text: “Go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.”
items.why: He uses Hosea to show that mercy was always the point of the law.

items.text: “But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil.”
items.why: The law limited revenge; Jesus asks for none. Some scholars call this fulfilling the law’s intent, so you could argue for that category too.

items.text: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness.”
items.why: Paul sees Christ as the goal (*telos*) the law was moving toward.
Paul reads the wilderness story as a pattern that finds its meaning in Christ.

items.text: “Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives.”
items.why: Jesus names a provision of the law as a concession and points back past it to God’s original design.

items.text: “The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.”
items.why: Paul contrasts the covenant on stone with the life-giving Spirit of the risen Lord, who removes the veil.
Mark draws out that Jesus’ teaching sets aside the food laws as markers of purity.

voices.text: Whatever does not teach Christ is not yet apostolic, even though St. Peter or St. Paul does the teaching.
voices.source: Preface to the Epistles of St. James and St. Jude (1522)

views.name: Jesus fulfils and deepens the law (no contradiction)
views.who: D. A. Carson, Craig Keener, Douglas Moo, many Jewish New Testament scholars in different forms
views.summary: Jesus’ “but I say to you” sayings do not cancel Moses; they reveal the law’s deepest intention and correct narrow interpretations. Even “eye for an eye” was a limit for courts, not a licence for personal revenge, so Jesus is drawing out its merciful intent.
views.strengths: Fits Matt 5:17-19 closely; respects the Old Testament as God’s word; matches how Jewish teachers debated the meaning of the law.
views.critiques: Some scholars think it underplays places where Jesus clearly goes beyond the text (food laws, divorce concession) and the startling authority of “I say”.

views.name: Jesus as the authoritative interpreter who also moves beyond
views.who: Greg Boyd, Brian Zahnd, Peter Enns, Richard Hays (in a more traditional form)
views.summary: Jesus reads selectively and with sovereign freedom: he stops before “vengeance”, rejects Elijah’s fire, names Moses’ concession, and declares foods clean. He reveals that some earlier understandings of God and of God’s will were partial, and he is the measure.
views.strengths: Takes seriously the patterns across the Gospels taken together; explains why the apostles felt free to set aside food laws and circumcision for Gentiles.
views.critiques: Traditional readers say some examples are over-read (the Isaiah pause may be about timing) and that Jesus also upholds the law strongly and warns of judgement himself (Matt 5:18; Matt 25:31-46).

views.name: Paul read Scripture from Christ backwards
views.who: Richard Hays, N. T. Wright, Francis Watson
views.summary: Paul’s conversion did not make him abandon Israel’s Scriptures but reread them as the story of Israel’s God fulfilling his promises in the Messiah, with figural echoes and patterns (typology).
views.strengths: Explains Paul’s constant use of the Old Testament and his figural readings (1 Cor 10; Gal 4) without calling them arbitrary.
views.critiques: Some scholars think Paul’s readings are sometimes forced by modern standards; Jewish readers note that the same texts can be read without Jesus as their goal.

views.name: Jewish perspectives on Jesus’ debates
views.who: Amy-Jill Levine, Marc Zvi Brettler, David Flusser
views.summary: Jesus’ arguments about sabbath, purity and mercy are recognisable Jewish debates; teachers such as Hillel also put love of neighbour at the centre of the Torah. Jesus should be read as a Jew arguing within Judaism.
views.strengths: Corrects caricatures of Pharisees as heartless legalists; helps Christians hear Jesus in his own setting.
views.critiques: Christians hold that Jesus’ “I say to you” claims an authority greater than a rabbi’s, which these readings may underplay.

misreadings.topic: “Jesus came to abolish the Old Testament”
misreadings.popular: Jesus replaced the harsh Old Testament with a new message of love, so Christians can ignore the Old Testament.
misreadings.inContext: Jesus says he came “not to destroy, but to fulfil”. He quoted the Scriptures constantly and read them as being about himself. Love of God and neighbour, mercy and justice are already the heart of the Hebrew Bible (Deut 6:5; Lev 19:18; Mic 6:8). Jesus-lens writers stress that he brings the Scriptures to their goal; they do not discard them.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars add that Jesus affirmed the law down to the smallest letter (Matt 5:18) and that the Old Testament remains Christian Scripture (Rom 15:4; 2 Tim 3:16).
misreadings.whyItMatters: Dismissing the Old Testament loses the story that explains who Jesus is, and drifts toward Marcion’s ancient error.

misreadings.topic: “The letter kills” means “do not read literally”
misreadings.popular: 2 Cor 3:6 means we should look for hidden spiritual meanings and not take the words at face value.
misreadings.inContext: Paul is contrasting two covenants: the old, written on stone tablets, and the new, written by the Spirit on human hearts (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26). The “letter” is the law as an external written code without the Spirit’s life. It is not a rule about literal versus symbolic interpretation.
misreadings.defence: Both traditional and newer scholars largely agree on this; the difference lies in how much they think the old covenant’s written code still guides Christians.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Misreading this verse can justify ignoring what a text actually says, the very eisegesis this course warns against.

misreadings.topic: “The Pharisees were legalists who hated mercy”
misreadings.popular: Jesus’ sharp words show that the Jewish leaders of his day were hypocrites who taught salvation by rules.
misreadings.inContext: Jesus’ irony was aimed at particular ways of reading that put status and tradition above mercy — a danger in every religious community. Many Pharisees valued mercy, and Jesus himself says to do what they teach (Matt 23:2-3). Scholars such as E. P. Sanders and Amy-Jill Levine have shown how unfair the caricature is.
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars agree the caricature is unfair, while noting that the Gospels do record real, serious conflicts over authority and interpretation.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If we make “the Pharisees” the villains, we miss that Jesus’ warnings are aimed at us whenever we use the Bible to exclude.

discuss: Jesus said the Scriptures “testify of me” to people who studied them carefully. How can a person know the Bible well and still miss Jesus? Has that ever been true of you?
Look at the compare table. Which example surprises you most? Is Jesus fulfilling the text’s purpose, moving beyond it, or both?
Why do you think Jesus stopped reading before “the day of vengeance”? Which lens persuades you, and why?
Jesus called Moses’ divorce law a concession to hard hearts. Does that change how you read other Old Testament laws?
How did Paul’s encounter with the risen Christ change the way he read the same Scriptures he had always known?
Where might Christians today be “straining at gnats and swallowing camels” in how we use the Bible?
practice: Read Matthew 5:17-48 in one sitting. For each “you have heard… but I say”, look up the Old Testament text behind it and write one sentence on what Jesus does with it.
Read Luke 4:16-30 and Isaiah 61:1-3 side by side. Mark the line where Jesus stopped and notice what made the crowd angry.
Read 2 Corinthians 3 slowly. Each time you open the Bible this week, pray Paul’s words: “Lord, take away the veil.”

lessons.title: Jesus, the Word Who Interprets the Words
lessons.question: If Jesus is the Word of God, how does he interpret the words of Scripture? What does “Jesus is perfect theology” mean, and what are the fair objections to it?
lessons.bigIdea: The Bible calls Jesus the Word, the exact imprint of God’s nature, and the one who has “exegeted” the Father. Scripture bears witness to him; he is its centre, context and life. Christians agree on that; they disagree on how far the lens of Jesus reshapes our reading of the Old Testament’s portraits of God.

sections.heading: The Word before the words
sections.body:
John’s Gospel begins: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” The Greek word is *logos*. For Jewish readers it echoed the creating word of Genesis 1 (“And God said…”) and the figure of Wisdom who was with God at creation. For Greek readers *logos* meant reason, the order behind the world. John says this Word “was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”

So in the New Testament the primary “Word of God” is a person. The Scriptures are also rightly called the word of God, but they are words that bear witness to the Word. This is why Jesus could say to Bible experts, “Search the scriptures… they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” The life is not in the pages by themselves; it is in the one they point to.

The learner’s notes say it this way: Jesus is the context and the life of the Scriptures, and without the Word the Bible becomes deadly. Church history sadly supports the warning: crusades, inquisitions, slavery and apartheid were all defended by quoting verses. Texts cut off from the character of Jesus can be used to kill.

sections.heading: Jesus “exegeted” the Father (John 1:18)
sections.body:
John’s prologue ends: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.” The verb “declared” is *exēgēsato*, from *exēgeomai*, the root of our word “exegesis”. It means to lead out, to tell in full, to explain. Jesus is the full explanation of the Father.

There is a textual detail worth knowing. The oldest manuscripts (including two early papyri, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus) read “the only begotten God” (*monogenēs theos*); many later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “the only begotten Son”. Either way, John claims that the one who is closest to the Father — “in his bosom”, the same picture used of the beloved disciple leaning on Jesus at the supper — has made him known.

Jesus says the same in his own words: “He that hath seen me hath seen the Father.” That is the foundation of the Jesus lens.

sections.heading: The exact imprint: Hebrews 1:3 and Colossians
sections.body:
Hebrews says the Son is “the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.” “Express image” translates *charaktēr*, a word for the mark a stamp or seal leaves in wax or metal — the image on a coin that exactly matches the die. It appears only here in the New Testament. The Son is not a rough sketch of God; he is God’s own imprint in a human life.

Paul says the same in other words: Christ “is the image (*eikōn*) of the invisible God”; “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily”; God’s glory shines “in the face of Jesus Christ”. The archbishop Michael Ramsey summed it up in a line that Jesus-lens writers love to quote: God is Christlike, and in him is no un-Christlikeness at all.

This is what Bill Johnson means by his phrase “Jesus Christ is perfect theology”: if you want to know what God is like — his will to heal, forgive and restore — look at Jesus. It does not mean Jesus is the only thing we learn about God; it means nothing true about God can contradict him.

sections.heading: “If a reading gives a Father unlike the Son…”
sections.body:
The Jesus lens draws a practical rule from these texts. Tommy Miller puts it in three statements: the human, the Father and creation’s destiny are each “unknowable apart from the saving incarnation of Jesus Christ.” Before Christ, humanity guessed at what a human might be; Jesus is “the human”. The Old Testament holds types, shadows, poems and dreams, but “the Father’s face is fully revealed in the Son’s face.” And creation’s future is revealed when “the true human stands up”. Then he reverses all three: “in Jesus, the human is fully known, the Father is fully known, and creation’s future is fully known.”

From this comes the test: “If a reading of Scripture gives you a Father who is unlike the Son, your reading is incorrect.” On this view the Old Testament is not the biography of a different, angrier God. It is an inspired, honest record of a people’s developing and often partial perception of the one God who has always been like Jesus — “through a glass, darkly”. God accommodated himself to people with “hardness of heart”, met them where they were, and let his reputation be bruised by their perceptions in order to stay in relationship. In Jesus, God says, in effect, “Let me show you who I have been all along.”

This view also answers three objections. To “you ignore the plain text”, it replies: we read with the key the text gives, as Jesus did in Matthew 5. To “this is reading Christ into texts”, it replies: Jesus himself said the Scriptures testify of him. To “this makes the Old Testament irrelevant”, it replies: it makes it permanently relevant as the story Christ fulfils — he is the “yes” to all God’s promises.

sections.heading: Fair objections, and the replies
sections.body:
Every serious Christian tradition agrees that Christ is the centre of Scripture. The disagreement is about what that means for Old Testament texts that portray God differently. The main objections are these.

The Marcion risk. In the second century Marcion taught that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser god, and he cut the Scriptures down to an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. The church rejected this firmly (Irenaeus and Tertullian wrote against him). Critics warn that saying some Old Testament portraits of God are “human misperception” can lead the same way. Jesus-lens writers reply that they affirm one God and the whole canon as inspired; what they reject is reading those texts without Jesus.

Jesus affirmed the Old Testament. He said not one jot or tittle of the law would pass, that “the scripture cannot be broken”, and he spoke of the flood and Sodom as real judgements. Critics also note that the New Testament has its own judgement texts, from Jesus’ parables of judgement to Ananias and Sapphira and the book of Revelation. Replies vary: some Jesus-lens writers read New Testament judgement as God handing people over to the consequences they choose (Rom 1:24-28); others accept final judgement while insisting it is the judgement of the crucified Lamb.

Who decides what is Christlike? Critics ask whether “Christlike” can become a mirror of our own preferences. Defenders answer that the criterion is not a feeling but the specific Jesus of the Gospels, especially the cross, and that this protects against importing modern values. Jewish readers add another concern: describing Israel’s Scriptures as a record of “flawed perception” can sound like a put-down of Judaism, which has read the same texts faithfully for millennia. Any Christ-centred reading has to answer that with humility.

sections.heading: Other Christ-centred readings that keep the Old Testament as true revelation
sections.body:
It is important to know that many Reformed and evangelical scholars are also strongly Christ-centred, but in a different way. Graeme Goldsworthy (*Gospel and Kingdom*, *According to Plan*) and Edmund Clowney (*The Unfolding Mystery*, *Preaching Christ in All of Scripture*) teach that every part of the Old Testament points to Christ through promise, pattern and story. Christopher J. H. Wright (*Knowing Jesus Through the Old Testament*) shows how Jesus’ own identity and mission come from Israel’s Scriptures. N. T. Wright reads the whole Bible as one drama whose climax is Jesus.

For these writers, Jesus is the lens that brings the Old Testament into focus, not a lens that filters some of it out. The flood, the exodus judgements and the conquest are read as real acts of God’s justice that foreshadow the cross, where judgement and mercy meet. Paul Copan and others argue that many hard texts use the exaggerated war language common in the ancient world, and are less brutal than they first appear.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold together both sides in their own way: Christ is the key to the whole Scripture, read within the church’s worship and the teaching of the Fathers, and the Old Testament contains “incomplete and temporary” elements that still belong to God’s teaching plan (*Dei Verbum* 15). The question for every reader is not whether to read through Jesus, but how.

visuals.title: *exēgeomai*: Jesus explains the Father
visuals.intro: The verb behind “he hath declared him” in John 1:18. It occurs six times in the New Testament.

senses.meaning: To tell in full, to narrate
senses.note: The common sense in Luke and Acts: to recount events step by step.

senses.meaning: To report what God has done
senses.note: Used of Barnabas and Paul telling the signs God did among the Gentiles, and of James reporting how God visited the Gentiles.

senses.meaning: To make known, to explain, to interpret
senses.note: In wider Greek it was used of interpreting sacred things, which is how “exegesis” came to mean explaining a text. John says the Son has made the unseen Father known: Jesus is the Father’s exegesis.

visuals.title: *charaktēr*: the exact imprint
visuals.intro: Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son “the express image of his person”. The Greek word occurs only here in the New Testament.

senses.meaning: A tool for engraving or stamping
senses.note: From a verb meaning to cut or engrave; first the die or seal itself.

The image stamped on a coin or pressed into wax, which matches the die exactly. Hebrews pairs it with “brightness” (*apaugasma*, radiance) and says the Son is the imprint of God’s very being (*hypostasis*).
Our English word “character” comes from it. The idea: the Son shows exactly what God is like.

visuals.title: Jesus at the centre of the Scriptures
visuals.intro: How the parts of Scripture relate to Jesus, according to the New Testament. Tap a node for the texts.

nodes.label: Jesus, the Word
nodes.detail: The Word made flesh, the exact imprint of God, the one who has explained the Father.

nodes.label: The Law
nodes.detail: Moses wrote of him; the law was a guardian until Christ, and he is its goal.

nodes.label: The Prophets
nodes.detail: They searched for the salvation and the sufferings of the Messiah; Jesus read Isaiah as fulfilled in him.

nodes.label: Psalms and writings
nodes.detail: Jesus named the psalms as speaking of him and prayed them on the cross.

nodes.label: Types and shadows
nodes.detail: Patterns such as the Passover, the rock and the temple are shadows; the reality is Christ.

nodes.label: Promises
nodes.detail: All God’s promises find their “yes” in him.

nodes.label: The Gospels
nodes.detail: The witness to his life, death and resurrection: the centre of the canon.

nodes.label: Apostolic letters
nodes.detail: The apostles explain what his death and resurrection mean and reread the Scriptures in his light.

nodes.label: The Spirit
nodes.detail: The Spirit inspired the Scriptures and takes what is Christ’s and makes it known; the Spirit removes the veil.

nodes.label: The reader today
nodes.detail: We read the whole Bible as witnesses to him, so that we may come to him and have life.

nodes.label: The Father revealed
nodes.detail: Whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father.

visuals.title: Reading Matthew 5:38-48 through different lenses
visuals.intro: “An eye for an eye… But I say unto you… Love your enemies… that ye may be the children of your Father.”
visuals.passage: Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: but I say unto you, That ye resist not evil… Love your enemies… that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good… Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.

lenses.name: Jesus lens
lenses.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd
lenses.reading: Jesus grounds enemy-love in the Father’s own character. If the Father loves enemies, then portrayals of God commanding merciless violence must be read through this revelation, as accommodation to an earlier, partial perception.

lenses.name: Fulfilment of the law’s intent
lenses.reading: “Eye for eye” limited punishment in court; it never commanded personal revenge. Jesus applies the law’s merciful purpose to personal relationships. The Old Testament also commands kindness to enemies (Exod 23:4-5; Prov 25:21).

lenses.name: Christ-centred salvation history
lenses.reading: The kingdom has come in Jesus, so his people now live by its ethic. Past judgements were real acts of God’s justice; final judgement remains, and belongs to God, which frees believers to love enemies (Rom 12:19-21).

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.reading: Rabbis also read “eye for an eye” as monetary compensation, not literal maiming. Jesus’ teaching stands within Jewish debates about mercy, while making a strong call to non-retaliation.

voices.source: Phrase used widely in his preaching; also the title of his book *Jesus Christ Is Perfect Theology* (2016)

voices.text: If a reading of Scripture gives you a Father who is unlike the Son, your reading is incorrect. Scripture bears witness to the Word; it is not the Word himself (John 5:39–40). Jesus is the measure that measures all.
Now reverse all three: in Jesus, the human is fully known, the Father is fully known, and creation’s future is fully known. God is not hiding behind mystery. He is unveiling in the Son.

views.name: Jesus is perfect theology (cruciform Jesus lens)
views.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Eric Seibert (in a stronger form), Tommy Miller, Bill Johnson (the phrase)
views.summary: Jesus, and above all the cross, is the full and final revelation of God. Any portrait of God, including in Scripture, must be measured by him. Old Testament portraits that do not look like Jesus are read as God accommodating himself to his people’s partial perceptions.
views.strengths: Builds directly on John 1:18, John 14:9, Heb 1:3 and Col 2:9; offers a coherent way to read violent texts; gives believers confidence that God is good; echoes church fathers such as Origen and Gregory of Nyssa who read some texts spiritually because they seemed unworthy of God.
views.critiques: Risk of Marcionism; Jesus himself affirmed the Old Testament and spoke of judgement; the New Testament has its own judgement texts; the criterion of “Christlikeness” may be shaped by the reader’s values.

views.name: Christ-centred salvation history (Reformed and evangelical)
views.who: Graeme Goldsworthy, Edmund Clowney, Christopher J. H. Wright, D. A. Carson, Tim Keller
views.summary: Every part of Scripture points to Christ through promise, pattern and story. The Old Testament’s portrayals of God, including his judgements, are true revelation, which Christ fulfils (judgement and mercy meet at the cross).
views.strengths: Holds the whole canon as fully true; follows Luke 24:27; keeps God’s justice and love together; strong guard against Marcionism.
views.critiques: Jesus-lens writers say it leaves God’s character divided (Jesus loving enemies, God commanding their destruction) and can explain away the force of Jesus’ “but I say to you”.

views.name: Hard texts as ancient war rhetoric
views.who: Paul Copan, Matthew Flannagan, John Walton
views.summary: Many violent texts use the stylised, exaggerated language of ancient Near Eastern war reports, and much of the Torah improved on surrounding laws. Read in context, God is not the moral monster some suppose.
views.strengths: Takes the ancient setting seriously; keeps the texts as true revelation while softening misreadings; based on comparative evidence.
views.critiques: Critics on both sides say it does not remove the moral problem, only reduces it; Jesus-lens writers think it still leaves God commanding killing.

views.name: Catholic and Orthodox: Christ the key, read in the church
views.who: *Dei Verbum*; Origen, Augustine, Maximus the Confessor; John Behr
views.summary: Christ is the key that opens all Scripture, which is read in the church’s worship and in the line of the Fathers. The Old Testament contains elements that are “incomplete and temporary” yet belong to God’s pedagogy, and the spiritual sense of texts finds Christ throughout.
views.strengths: Deep historical roots; integrates Christ-centred reading with the creeds and worship; avoids both Marcion and literalism.
views.critiques: Protestants worry that tradition may overrule Scripture; some find allegorical readings too loose to check.

views.name: Jewish concerns
views.who: Jon Levenson, Amy-Jill Levine, Marc Zvi Brettler
views.summary: The Hebrew Bible has its own integrity and was read faithfully by Jews for centuries before and after Jesus. Treating it as “partial” or “flawed perception” can echo old Christian contempt for Judaism.
views.strengths: Calls Christians to humility and accuracy; reminds them that Jesus and the apostles were Jews reading Jewish Scripture.
views.critiques: Christians answer that confessing Jesus as the fullest revelation is not contempt for Israel, whose Scriptures Paul calls a privilege (Rom 9:4-5).

misreadings.topic: “The Word of God” always means the Bible
misreadings.popular: When the Bible says “the Word of God”, it is talking about the Bible itself.
misreadings.inContext: In John 1 and Rev 19:13 the Word is a person, Jesus. Elsewhere “the word of God” often means God’s message preached (Acts 4:31; Acts 6:7). The Scriptures are God’s word in the sense that they bear witness to the Word and carry his message.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree that Jesus is the Word in the fullest sense, while insisting that Scripture is truly God’s word written (2 Tim 3:16; Mark 7:13), not merely a human witness.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Forgetting that the Word is a person can turn Bible reading into rule-checking that never comes to Jesus for life (John 5:39-40).

misreadings.popular: Anyone who reads Old Testament violence through Jesus is rejecting the Old Testament God, like Marcion.
misreadings.inContext: Marcion taught two different gods and cut most Scripture out of his canon. Jesus-lens writers such as Boyd and Jersak confess one God, keep the whole canon, and say the problem is in the human perception, not a different god. The charge is a real warning but not an accurate description of their view.
misreadings.defence: Critics reply that, even with one God and one canon, saying some texts misrepresent God functionally does what Marcion did: it lets the reader decide which parts of Scripture really speak for God.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Labels end conversations. The fair question is whether a reading keeps both one God and the authority of the whole canon.

discuss: What is the difference between calling Jesus “the Word” and calling the Bible “the word of God”? Why does it matter which comes first?
John says Jesus “exegeted” the Father. If you had only Jesus’ life to go on, what would you say God is like?
Tommy Miller says that if a reading gives a Father unlike the Son, the reading is wrong. Where does that test help you? Where might it be hard to apply?

Which objection to the Jesus lens do you find strongest: the Marcion risk, Jesus’ own high view of the Old Testament, New Testament judgement texts, or “who decides what is Christlike”? How would you answer it?
How do Goldsworthy and Clowney’s Christ-centred readings differ from Boyd and Jersak’s? What does each one protect?
Can you think of a time when the Bible was used in a way that was “deadly”? What would reading through Jesus have changed?
practice: Read John 1:1-18 aloud. Underline every phrase that says what the Word does, and write a one-line prayer from verse 18.
Choose one hard Old Testament passage. Read it, then read a Gospel passage that shows Jesus in a similar situation. Write down what you learn from the comparison and what questions remain.
With a friend who reads differently from you, take one view in the views list and try to explain it so well that its holder would say, “Yes, that is what I believe.”
